title: ICE Collected Nearly 1 Million People’s DNA Last Year—Including Young Children
gist: Georgetown Law's Center on Privacy and Technology, working from FOIA'd ICE training slides and CBP spreadsheets, estimates ICE alone pushed as many as 919,908 new genetic profiles into the FBI's CODIS 'detainee' index in 2025 — making DHS the single largest source of new profiles in the US criminal DNA system, mostly from people with no criminal conviction. An internal ICE lawyer's email stating the program's 'primary purpose' is building 'a national DNA database for solving crimes' undercuts the booking-identification rationale that made the collection legally defensible under Maryland v. King, while CBP records show 492 children under 14 — including 5- and 6-year-olds — were sent to the FBI in a single year.

insights.claim: The FBI's CODIS 'detainee' sub-index, where DHS-collected genetic profiles are stored, reached 3,345,692 profiles by December 2025 after growing by roughly 995,000 in that year alone — a run rate of more than 2,700 new profiles per day.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A federal biometric database compounding at ~1M records/year is a step-change in demand for forensic sequencing capacity, sample storage and lab throughput — watch the federal forensic-genomics contracting pipeline.
insights.quote: That is more than 2,700 people a day, every day, for a year.
insights.locator: Georgetown's new report suggests the program

insights.claim: Because CBP submitted only about 75,215 people's DNA to the FBI in 2025, Georgetown attributes the residual — as many as 919,908 new CODIS profiles in a single year — to ICE, making the Department of Homeland Security the largest single source of new genetic profiles in the US criminal DNA system.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
entities: Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology
insights.so_what: Immigration enforcement, not criminal justice, is now the dominant intake channel for the national criminal DNA system — a structural fact that reframes the political and legal risk attached to the whole database.
insights.quote: Based on the gap, Georgetown estimates that ICE may be responsible for as many as 919,908 new profiles in a single year.
insights.locator: The FBI does not explicitly disclose which agency

insights.claim: Profiles from people detained under federal authority were a negligible share of the searchable CODIS index before 2020 and about 9 percent by 2024; at current collection rates Georgetown projects DHS will have supplied more than a third of that index by 2030 — four years earlier than its own prior 2034 estimate.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
entities: Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology
insights.so_what: The forecast was pulled forward four years in one revision — a signal that the acceleration is outrunning the analysts tracking it, and that legal challenges will land against a much larger installed base than expected.
insights.quote: DHS will have supplied more than a third of that index by 2030—a milestone it had previously estimated wouldn't arrive until 2034.

themes.theme: ICE displaces CBP as the collection engine

insights.claim: ICE was a marginal DNA collector as recently as fiscal 2021, taking 3,609 samples in FY2020 and 16,392 more through mid-May of FY2021 — roughly 20,000 in total — while CBP sent the FBI the DNA of at least 1.36 million people between October 2020 and the end of 2024.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
entities: Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology
insights.so_what: Establishes the baseline: ICE's 2025 output is roughly 45x its entire early-program cumulative total, so the 2025 number is a regime change rather than trend growth.
insights.locator: For most of the program's history, migrant DNA collection

insights.claim: The locus of US immigration detention has flipped from the border to the interior — ICE now accounts for roughly 85 percent of immigration detentions versus CBP's 15 percent, reversing the historical split — which mechanically relocates DNA collection from ports of entry to interior arrests.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Interior enforcement, not border encounters, is now the volume driver for biometric intake — the growth is decoupled from migration flows and tied instead to domestic arrest policy.
insights.locator: The change tracks a broader shift.

insights.claim: ICE was holding 65,765 people as of July 11, up from 60,311 in early April, with arrests climbing toward 1,500 a day, and the largest single group in detention had no criminal history at all.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Detention population and arrest velocity are the leading indicators for CODIS intake; rising detention capacity translates directly into database growth and into revenue for detention operators and biometric processing vendors.
insights.quote: The largest single group in detention had no criminal history at all.
insights.locator: As of July 11 of this year, ICE was holding

insights.claim: The FBI does not disclose which agency submitted which CODIS profile and ICE has refused repeated public records requests for comparable data, so the scale of ICE's contribution is knowable only as a residual estimate derived from CBP's disclosed numbers.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
entities: Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology
insights.so_what: Attribution opacity is the program's main defense: without agency-level disclosure, oversight bodies and litigants must argue from inference, which slows any legal or legislative constraint.
insights.quote: ICE has refused to release comparable data, rebuffing repeated public records requests.
insights.locator: The FBI does not explicitly disclose which agency

insights.claim: Congress authorized federal DNA collection from people arrested, charged, convicted or detained under federal authority back in 2005, but Justice Department regulations let DHS exempt many immigration detainees on resource-burden grounds — meaning the binding constraint on mass collection was regulatory, not statutory.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A program of this scale was switched on by a rule change, not legislation — so it can be switched off the same way, without Congress, making it far more sensitive to executive turnover than a statutory program.
insights.locator: US law enforcement’s increased DNA collection traces

insights.claim: The DOJ eliminated the resource-burden exemption in 2020, and that December ICE issued Directive 10092.1 requiring officers to collect DNA from nearly everyone in its custody — the two acts that converted a discretionary program into near-universal collection.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: The causal chain from rule change to ~1M profiles/year is short and documented — a template for how fast a biometric mandate can scale once an administrative carve-out is removed.
insights.locator: In 2020, the DOJ eliminated the exemption.

insights.claim: FOIA'd May 2021 ICE training materials instructed Enforcement and Removal Operations officers that asylum seekers and refugees who have not adjusted status are not exempt from DNA collection, and told them in capital letters to collect after 'ANY arrest' — evidence the policy was taught as maximally broad from the outset.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
entities: Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology
insights.so_what: Internal training documents, not public policy statements, define the real operating rule — the gap between the two is where litigation discovery finds leverage.
insights.quote: therefore, their DNA must be sampled.
insights.locator: Internal 2021 training materials obtained by Georgetown

insights.claim: The legal foundation for warrantless DNA collection from detainees is Maryland v. King, in which the Supreme Court upheld swabbing arrestees partly because the state framed it as establishing identity and criminal history during booking rather than investigating unrelated crimes — an identification rationale the DOJ reused in 2020 for immigration detainees.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: The whole program rests on one characterization — 'this is fingerprinting, not investigation.' If that characterization fails in court, the collection authority and the retained samples are both exposed.
insights.locator: Primary Purpose

insights.claim: An attorney in ICE's Office of the Principal Legal Advisor wrote in a March 2025 legal opinion that the 'primary purpose' of the government's DNA-collection authority is to build 'a national DNA database for solving crimes,' not to establish family relationships — the government's own lawyer contradicting the identification rationale used to defend the program.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
entities: Office of the Principal Legal Advisor
insights.so_what: This is the single most legally damaging document in the report — an admission against interest that plaintiffs in Fourth Amendment suits will cite directly, and DHS declined to respond when asked whether it agreed.
insights.quote: a national DNA database for solving crimes
insights.locator: In late March 2025, a deputy official at ICE

insights.claim: Georgetown's research director argues the constitutional defect is suspicionless compulsion for speculative future crime-solving, and that the internal ICE email proves that is precisely the program's design rather than an incidental effect.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
entities: Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology
insights.so_what: Frames the coming litigation theory: not 'was this person lawfully arrested' but 'is warrantless retention for future searches constitutional at all' — a ruling on that would reach far beyond immigration.
insights.quote: The Fourth Amendment categorically prohibits the government from compelling you, without suspicion, to hand over your sensitive information on the speculation that it might be helpful for crime-solving in the future
insights.locator: Stevie Glaberson, research director at Georgetown Law

insights.claim: A May 2021 ICE presentation counted 69 confirmed CODIS hits from ERO-submitted samples in roughly six months under a heading reading 'FUN FACTS,' listing matches in sexual offense, homicide, missing person, burglary, larceny and stalking cases plus a stolen Pinto — showing the agency's internal success metric was crime-solving hits, not identification.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Corroborates the 'primary purpose' email from a different document and a different year: the program measures itself by crime hits, which is the exact use the identification rationale disclaims.
insights.quote: Editor's note: you'd care if that was YOUR Pinto!
insights.locator: Fun Facts

insights.claim: Physical DNA samples taken from immigration detainees — each containing a person's entire genome — are retained in a federal laboratory indefinitely, and the derived profiles can be compared against crime-scene evidence collected years or decades in the future.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Indefinite retention of whole genomes creates a permanent, expanding liability surface — the value and risk of the archive grow with every advance in genomic inference technique, not just with database size.
insights.quote: The physical sample, which holds a person's entire genome, sits in a federal laboratory indefinitely.
insights.locator: Yet once the DNA profiles of detained people enter

insights.claim: Refusing to provide DNA in federal custody is a misdemeanor that ICE itself said in 2021 it was unaware had ever been accepted for prosecution, but WIRED identified two prosecutions filed in 2025 against people in immigration custody — both of which ended in conviction or guilty plea with time-served sentences.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A dormant statute becoming live prosecution converts a paper threat into real compliance leverage — this is the enforcement mechanism that makes near-universal collection achievable in practice.
insights.locator: ICE training materials instruct officers to warn people

insights.claim: In the Puerto Rico case, CBP officers asked Ronald Genao-Diaz for a DNA sample on at least five separate occasions and he refused each time, covering his mouth with a disposable mask; after a probable cause finding he pleaded guilty, provided the sample during Bureau of Prisons processing, and received time served plus a fine.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Illustrates that refusal only delays collection — the sample is taken downstream anyway, so the prosecution serves deterrence rather than acquisition, which is the more coercive read.

themes.theme: Children entering the criminal DNA index

insights.claim: DHS told Representatives Joaquin Castro, Greg Stanton and Nanette Barragán in correspondence that ICE may collect DNA from children as young as 14, and confirmed that samples collected under the program are sent to the FBI for analysis and entry into CODIS.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A written departmental admission that minors' profiles enter the criminal index removes the ambiguity defenders relied on and gives Congress a concrete hook for legislation or appropriations riders.
insights.quote: They do not belong in a database meant for violent criminals, especially children.
insights.locator: Kids, Tested

insights.claim: Newly released CBP records identify 492 children under 14 whose DNA the agency sent to the FBI between January 2025 and January 2026 — including 33 seven-year-olds, 32 six-year-olds and 21 five-year-olds — showing federal agencies breached even their own stated 14-year age floor.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
entities: Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology
insights.so_what: Documented violation of the agency's own stated limit is the fact most likely to force an inspector general review or injunction — it converts a policy dispute into a compliance failure.
insights.locator: Federal immigration agencies have not always followed

insights.claim: Flores settlement counsel who have visited the reopened Dilley family detention center 12 times report that families 'regularly' say they were DNA tested without being told why, cannot determine what criteria ICE applies, and often never learn the results — and ICE offered members of Congress conflicting explanations for why samples were taken, where they went and how long they would be kept.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Procedural opacity plus conflicting official accounts is exactly the fact pattern that survives a motion to dismiss — and the Flores counsel's inspection rights give plaintiffs a standing evidence pipeline.
insights.quote: I honestly don’t know why they’re taking the DNA,
insights.locator: Welch says Flores settlement–related counsel cannot yet

insights.claim: DHS deflected questions about children's CODIS profiles by pointing to a separate DNA program used to verify family relationships — a program distinct from the CODIS collection at issue — and at least one detained 12-year-old's account of testing 'for security reasons' and to prove paternity is more consistent with familial verification than CODIS collection.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Two overlapping DNA programs let the agency answer questions about one by describing the other; any credible oversight has to force per-sample attribution before the topline numbers can be contested or confirmed.
insights.locator: Asked about children whose profiles were submitted to CODIS

themes.theme: Oversight vacuum and the litigation vector

insights.claim: DHS inspector general Joseph Cuffari told Representative Ayanna Pressley at a July 2025 congressional hearing that his office had 'just got done writing' a report on DNA collection from children, but a subsequent FOIA request produced two unrelated documents and identified no completed report, no draft, and no records showing the office had examined the program at all.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
entities: Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology
insights.so_what: The designated internal watchdog appears to have produced nothing while testifying otherwise — meaning constraint on this program will have to come from courts or appropriations, not from IG review.
insights.locator: Questions about the program’s oversight have grown

insights.claim: Months after ICE began collecting DNA from families at Dilley, the agency told members of Congress it was unaware of any assessment ever conducted of the privacy or civil-rights consequences of the practice.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: No privacy impact assessment on a program adding ~1M genomes a year is itself a procedural cause of action and the cheapest lever for a future administration or court to halt collection.
insights.quote: ICE said it was unaware of any such assessment.
insights.locator: Months after ICE began collecting DNA from families

insights.claim: In May 2026 four US citizens sued federal agencies in Briggs v. Mullin alleging agents took their DNA after detaining them at protests outside the Broadview, Illinois ICE facility during Operation Midway Blitz; the suit argues the collection program violates both the Fourth and First Amendments and seeks destruction of samples and expungement of profiles.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: US-citizen protester plaintiffs with dismissed charges are the strongest available test case, and the expungement remedy — if granted — would establish that CODIS entries can be unwound, undermining the database's permanence.
insights.quote: My charges were thrown out, but my private biological information is sitting in a lab somewhere.
insights.locator: In May 2026, four US citizens sued federal agencies

insights.claim: DHS's response to the protester allegations cited 28 CFR 28.12(b) requiring DNA collection from people arrested for federal crimes 'including rioters,' but did not address whether all plaintiffs were charged with such crimes, whether their profiles entered CODIS, or the broader findings on detainees and children.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: The department's consistent pattern of answering a narrower question than the one asked is a tell that the broad-collection conduct has no prepared legal defense — watch for that gap to be exploited in discovery.
insights.quote: Federal law requires law enforcement to collect DNA samples from individuals arrested for federal crimes under 28 CFR 28.12(b), including rioters arrested for assaulting or obstructing law enforcement,
insights.locator: Asked by Georgetown about those allegations

insights.claim: A separate suit was brought by George Retes Jr., an Army veteran working as a security guard at a California cannabis farm who says federal agents unlawfully detained him after a raid and took a cheek swab without explaining why the DNA was collected or what would happen to it.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: A second, independently-counseled case from a sympathetic US-citizen plaintiff signals the litigation is broadening beyond immigration advocacy groups into libertarian public-interest firms — a wider coalition than DHS likely priced in.
insights.locator: A separate lawsuit involves George Retes Jr.
